claim: Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) causes chickenpox.
source: Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) causes chickenpox and reactivation of latent VZV causes herpes zoster (HZ).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is established scientific knowledge.

claim: Reactivation of latent VZV causes herpes zoster (HZ).
source: Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) causes chickenpox and reactivation of latent VZV causes herpes zoster (HZ).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is established scientific knowledge.

claim: VZV reactivation is subject to declining VZV-specific cellular mediated immunity (CMI).
source: VZV reactivation is subject to the opposing mechanisms of declining and boosted VZV-specific cellular mediated immunity (CMI).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known mechanism.

claim: VZV reactivation is subject to boosted VZV-specific cellular mediated immunity (CMI).
source: VZV reactivation is subject to the opposing mechanisms of declining and boosted VZV-specific cellular mediated immunity (CMI).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known mechanism.

claim: A reduction in exogenous re-exposure opportunities through universal chickenpox vaccination could lead to an increase in HZ incidence.
source: A reduction in exogenous re-exposure 'opportunities' through universal chickenpox vaccination could therefore lead to an increase in HZ incidence.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the abstract based on the exogenous boosting mechanism.

claim: This is the first individual-based model that integrates within-host data on VZV-CMI and between-host transmission data to simulate HZ incidence.
source: We present the first individual-based model that integrates within-host data on VZV-CMI and between-host transmission data to simulate HZ incidence.
evidence: This is a direct claim about the novelty of the presented model.

claim: The duration of exogenous boosting is estimated at 2 years.
source: This model allows estimating currently unknown pivotal biomedical parameters, including the duration of exogenous boosting at 2 years, with a peak threefold to fourfold increase of VZV-CMI
evidence: This is a model-derived estimate presented in the abstract.

claim: Exogenous boosting causes a peak threefold to fourfold increase of VZV-CMI.
source: This model allows estimating currently unknown pivotal biomedical parameters, including the duration of exogenous boosting at 2 years, with a peak threefold to fourfold increase of VZV-CMI
evidence: This is a model-derived estimate presented in the abstract.

claim: The VZV weekly reactivation probability is 5%.
source: the VZV weekly reactivation probability at 5%
evidence: This is a model-derived estimate presented in the abstract.

claim: VZV subclinical reactivation has no effect on VZV-CMI.
source: VZV subclinical reactivation having no effect on VZV-CMI
evidence: This is a model-derived finding presented in the abstract.

claim: A 100% effective chickenpox vaccine given to 1 year olds would cause a 1.75 times peak increase in HZ 31 years after implementation.
source: A 100% effective chickenpox vaccine given to 1 year olds would cause a 1.75 times peak increase in HZ 31 years after implementation.
evidence: This is a model prediction presented in the abstract.

claim: The predicted increase in HZ following chickenpox vaccination is predicted to occur mainly in younger age groups than is currently assumed.
source: This increase is predicted to occur mainly in younger age groups than is currently assumed.
evidence: This is a model prediction presented in the abstract.

claim: VZV causes varicella or chickenpox, mainly during childhood.
source: Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) causes the itching, erythematous vesicular disease called varicella or chickenpox, mainly during childhood, and remains latent in neural ganglia afterwards.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge stated in the introduction.

claim: VZV remains latent in neural ganglia after primary infection.
source: Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) causes the itching, erythematous vesicular disease called varicella or chickenpox, mainly during childhood, and remains latent in neural ganglia afterwards.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge stated in the introduction.

claim: VZV can reactivate subclinically as shown by detection of VZV in saliva or blood from otherwise healthy individuals.
source: Latency can then be interrupted by episodes of (primarily subclinical) reactivation of VZV as shown by the detection of VZV in saliva or blood from otherwise healthy individuals (Schünemann et al., 1998; Nagel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: VZV reactivations may cause herpes zoster (HZ), which presents clinically as a painful dermatomal rash.
source: VZV reactivations may also cause herpes zoster (HZ), which presents clinically as a painful dermatomal rash.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge stated in the introduction.

claim: HZ occurs most frequently in individuals with a drastically declined cellular immune status.
source: HZ occurs most frequently in individuals with a drastically declined cellular immune status (Dolin et al., 1978)
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: Ageing itself is often assumed to substantially reduce resilience of the VZV-specific immune response.
source: but ageing itself is often assumed to substantially reduce resilience of the VZV-specific immune response (Miller, 1980; Berger et al., 1981; Levin et al., 2003, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: Waning of VZV cellular mediated immunity (CMI) by age is influenced by cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection.
source: Recent research supports the hypothesis that waning of VZV cellular mediated immunity (CMI) by age is also influenced by cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection (Ogunjimi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: Effective and safe pediatric vaccines against varicella exist.
source: Effective and safe pediatric vaccines against varicella exist and have been universally implemented in some countries including the US, Australia, Greece, Germany, Japan and Taiwan (Marin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference and is established knowledge.

claim: Varicella vaccines have been universally implemented in the US, Australia, Greece, Germany, Japan and Taiwan.
source: Effective and safe pediatric vaccines against varicella exist and have been universally implemented in some countries including the US, Australia, Greece, Germany, Japan and Taiwan (Marin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Policy makers in many countries have been hesitant to introduce childhood VZV vaccination due to the general population's perception of varicella as a relatively mild disease.
source: However, in many other countries policy makers have been hesitant to introduce childhood VZV vaccination due to the general population's perception of varicella as a relatively mild disease, as well as the so-called exogenous boosting hypothesis (Hope-Simpson, 1965; Ogunjimi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a reason for policy hesitation with supporting citations.

claim: Policy makers have been hesitant to introduce childhood VZV vaccination due to the exogenous boosting hypothesis.
source: However, in many other countries policy makers have been hesitant to introduce childhood VZV vaccination due to the general population's perception of varicella as a relatively mild disease, as well as the so-called exogenous boosting hypothesis (Hope-Simpson, 1965; Ogunjimi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a reason for policy hesitation with supporting citations.

claim: The exogenous boosting hypothesis is based on the concept of the secondary immune response.
source: This hypothesis is based on the concept of the secondary immune response and assumes that boosting of VZV-CMI occurs upon re-exposure to varicella.
evidence: This is an explanation of the hypothesis based on immunological knowledge.

claim: The exogenous boosting hypothesis assumes that boosting of VZV-CMI occurs upon re-exposure to varicella.
source: This hypothesis is based on the concept of the secondary immune response and assumes that boosting of VZV-CMI occurs upon re-exposure to varicella.
evidence: This is an explanation of the hypothesis.

claim: Boosted VZV-specific cellular immunity would reduce the risk of VZV reactivation and thence HZ.
source: Boosted VZV-specific cellular immunity would subsequently reduce the risk of VZV reactivation and thence HZ.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the exogenous boosting hypothesis.

claim: The introduction of widespread childhood VZV vaccination would reduce opportunities for varicella re-exposure.
source: The introduction of widespread childhood VZV vaccination would reduce opportunities for varicella re-exposure and could therefore increase HZ incidence, as shown in model-based projections (Schuette and Hethcote, 1999; Brisson et al., 2000; Bilcke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a logical inference supported by model-based projections.

claim: Widespread childhood VZV vaccination could increase HZ incidence, as shown in model-based projections.
source: The introduction of widespread childhood VZV vaccination would reduce opportunities for varicella re-exposure and could therefore increase HZ incidence, as shown in model-based projections (Schuette and Hethcote, 1999; Brisson et al., 2000; Bilcke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited model-based projections.

claim: A systematic review concluded that exogenous boosting exists.
source: Although current data on HZ-incidence post introduction of childhood VZV vaccination has caused controversy, a systematic review rating the quality of the evidence, concluded that exogenous boosting exists, but that its population-wide effect after widespread childhood VZV vaccination remains highly uncertain (Ogunjimi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a cited systematic review.

claim: The population-wide effect of exogenous boosting after widespread childhood VZV vaccination remains highly uncertain.
source: Although current data on HZ-incidence post introduction of childhood VZV vaccination has caused controversy, a systematic review rating the quality of the evidence, concluded that exogenous boosting exists, but that its population-wide effect after widespread childhood VZV vaccination remains highly uncertain (Ogunjimi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a cited systematic review.

claim: Current deterministic VZV simulation models entangle exogenous boosting, waning of immunity, immunosenescence and reactivation, undermining the possibility of estimating the magnitude and duration of exogenous boosting accurately.
source: One of the main points of criticism on current predictions by deterministic VZV simulation models is the entanglement of exogenous boosting, waning of immunity, immunosenescence and reactivation undermining the possibility of estimating the magnitude and duration of exogenous boosting accurately.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of existing models.

claim: Entangled parameters in deterministic models can be chosen to fit models well to observed HZ incidence data, but are too artificial to allow real and verifiable biological interpretations.
source: A concern is that these entangled parameters can be chosen to fit these models well to observed HZ incidence data, but that they are too artificial to allow real and verifiable biological interpretations.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of existing models.

claim: Some studies have shown VZV to reactivate subclinically in healthy individuals, immunocompromised and stressed individuals.
source: Indeed, some studies have shown VZV to reactivate subclinically both in healthy individuals, immunocompromised and stressed individuals (Schünemann et al., 1997; Mehta et al., 2003; Nagel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: The effect of subclinical VZV reactivation on VZV-CMI has not yet been quantified.
source: However, the effect on VZV-CMI has not yet been quantified.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: This is the first individual-based VZV model explicitly combining within and between-host dynamics.
source: In the current paper, we describe the first individual-based VZV model, explicitly combining within and between-host dynamics.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the presented model.

claim: The model is based on experimental viro-immunological data.
source: This model is based on experimental viro-immunological data and allows an accurate estimation of the exogenous boosting characteristics and explicit insertion or validation of experimental data.
evidence: This is a description of the model's foundation.

claim: Eight unique parameter sets led to a reasonable fit of Belgian HZ incidence data.
source: Using a step-wise algorithm we initially found eight unique parameter sets leading to a reasonable fit of Belgian HZ incidence data (see Table 1 and Figure 1).
evidence: This is a result from the model fitting procedure, supported by Table 1 and Figure 1.

claim: All best-fitting parameter sets were based on boosting scenario 3 (predefined exponential loss of boosted VZV-CMI).
source: All best-fitting parameter sets were based on boosting scenario 3 (predefined exponential loss of boosted VZV-CMI).
evidence: This is a result from the model fitting procedure.

claim: Seven of the best-fitting models include exogenous boosting with a peak value of 1.3.
source: Seven of these models include exogenous boosting (defined as an exponential decay) with a peak value of 1.3, a boosting duration ranging between 2 and 15 years, no endogenous boosting, a weekly VZV reactivation probability and an annual VZV-CMI loss (= waning) estimated to be 1–1.5% and 1–2%, respectively.
evidence: This is a result from the model fitting procedure.

claim: Seven of the best-fitting models have a boosting duration ranging between 2 and 15 years.
source: Seven of these models include exogenous boosting (defined as an exponential decay) with a peak value of 1.3, a boosting duration ranging between 2 and 15 years, no endogenous boosting, a weekly VZV reactivation probability and an annual VZV-CMI loss (= waning) estimated to be 1–1.5% and 1–2%, respectively.
evidence: This is a result from the model fitting procedure.

claim: Seven of the best-fitting models include no endogenous boosting.
source: Seven of these models include exogenous boosting (defined as an exponential decay) with a peak value of 1.3, a boosting duration ranging between 2 and 15 years, no endogenous boosting, a weekly VZV reactivation probability and an annual VZV-CMI loss (= waning) estimated to be 1–1.5% and 1–2%, respectively.
evidence: This is a result from the model fitting procedure.

claim: Seven of the best-fitting models have an annual VZV-CMI loss (waning) estimated to be 1–1.5%.
source: Seven of these models include exogenous boosting (defined as an exponential decay) with a peak value of 1.3, a boosting duration ranging between 2 and 15 years, no endogenous boosting, a weekly VZV reactivation probability and an annual VZV-CMI loss (= waning) estimated to be 1–1.5% and 1–2%, respectively.
evidence: This is a result from the model fitting procedure.

claim: The fits are excellent for age groups 25 years and older.
source: We note that although the fits are excellent for the most relevant age groups, 25 years and older, they are less suited to predict HZ incidence for younger ages.
evidence: This is an assessment of model fit quality.

claim: The initial fits are less suited to predict HZ incidence for younger ages.
source: We note that although the fits are excellent for the most relevant age groups, 25 years and older, they are less suited to predict HZ incidence for younger ages.
evidence: This is an assessment of model fit quality.

claim: One model predicted a peak boosting value of 2.5, a boosting duration of only 1 year and no endogenous boosting.
source: One model predicted a peak boosting value of 2.5, a boosting duration of only 1 year and no endogenous boosting.
evidence: This is a result from the model fitting procedure.

claim: The model with peak boosting value of 2.5 was less suited to fit to HZ data for older age groups but fitted much better to HZ data for younger age groups.
source: Although this model was less suited to fit to HZ data for older age groups, it fitted much better to HZ data for younger age groups.
evidence: This is an assessment of model fit quality.

claim: The two best fitting parameter sets predicted peak boosting values between 2.8 and 4.
source: The two best fitting parameter sets predicted peak boosting values between 2.8 and 4 (maximum allowable value), a duration of boosting limited to 1 or 2 years and, as before, no endogenous boosting.
evidence: This is a result from the refined model fitting procedure.

claim: The two best fitting parameter sets predicted a duration of boosting limited to 1 or 2 years.
source: The two best fitting parameter sets predicted peak boosting values between 2.8 and 4 (maximum allowable value), a duration of boosting limited to 1 or 2 years and, as before, no endogenous boosting.
evidence: This is a result from the refined model fitting procedure.

claim: The two best fitting parameter sets predicted no endogenous boosting.
source: The two best fitting parameter sets predicted peak boosting values between 2.8 and 4 (maximum allowable value), a duration of boosting limited to 1 or 2 years and, as before, no endogenous boosting.
evidence: This is a result from the refined model fitting procedure.

claim: The peak increase in HZ incidence was reached approximately 31 years after programme initiation.
source: The peak increase in HZ incidence was reached approximately 31 years after programme initiation and was 1.75 (1.64–1.87) (100% CI) times higher than the HZ incidence prior to varicella vaccination.
evidence: This is a model prediction for the vaccination scenario.

claim: The peak HZ incidence was 1.75 (1.64–1.87) times higher than the HZ incidence prior to varicella vaccination.
source: The peak increase in HZ incidence was reached approximately 31 years after programme initiation and was 1.75 (1.64–1.87) (100% CI) times higher than the HZ incidence prior to varicella vaccination.
evidence: This is a model prediction for the vaccination scenario with confidence interval.

claim: Per 1,000,000 person-years the total number of HZ cases would increase on average from 3219 to 5313 (set 9) or from 3209 to 5955 (set 13).
source: This means that per 1,000,000 person-years the total number of HZ cases would increase on average from 3219 to 5313 (set 9) or from 3209 to 5955 (set 13).
evidence: This is a model prediction for the vaccination scenario.

claim: The relative contribution of different age groups to HZ incidence changes in the time period after introduction of varicella vaccination.
source: Figure 5 shows that the relative contribution of different age groups to HZ incidence changes in the time period after introduction of varicella vaccination.
evidence: This is a model prediction shown in Figure 5.

claim: The 31–40 year old age group dominates HZ incidence between 10–50 years after introduction of varicella vaccination.
source: Noteworthy is the relative dominance of the 31–40 year old age group between 10–50 years after introduction of varicella vaccination.
evidence: This is a model prediction.

claim: This study is the first to use an individual-based dynamic transmission model for VZV.
source: To our knowledge, this study is the first to use an individual-based dynamic transmission model for VZV.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: The model allowed combining immunological and virological data to estimate key parameters in VZV population dynamics.
source: This model allowed us to combine immunological and virological data to estimate key parameters in VZV population dynamics, such as the peak CMI response following re-exposure, duration of boosting and VZV subclinical reactivation characteristics.
evidence: This is a description of the model's capabilities.

claim: The best fitting parameter sets for Belgium suggest the effective duration of exogenous boosting to last only between 1 and 2 years.
source: Our best fitting parameter sets for Belgium suggest the effective duration of exogenous boosting to last only between 1 and 2 years.
evidence: This is a model-derived estimate.

claim: The predicted duration of exogenous boosting (1-2 years) is significantly lower than the 20 years predicted by the deterministic VZV model by Brisson et al.
source: These predictions are significantly lower than those from the highly cited deterministic VZV model by Brisson et al., in which the average duration was predicted to be 20 years ([7–41 years] 95%CI) (Brisson et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a comparison with a cited model.

claim: The peak immunological response was estimated to be 2.8–4.0 times larger than the pre-re-exposure value.
source: Our peak immunological response was estimated to be 2.8–4.0 times larger than the pre-re-exposure value.
evidence: This is a model-derived estimate.

claim: The predicted peak immunological response (2.8-4.0 times) is consistent with those experimentally found in adults re-exposed to VZV by varicella contacts in the household.
source: These predictions are consistent with those experimentally found in adults re-exposed to VZV by varicella contacts in the household (Arvin et al., 1983; Vossen et al., 2004) or by vaccination (Levin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a comparison with cited experimental studies.

claim: The predicted peak immunological response (2.8-4.0 times) is consistent with those experimentally found in adults re-exposed to VZV by vaccination.
source: These predictions are consistent with those experimentally found in adults re-exposed to VZV by varicella contacts in the household (Arvin et al., 1983; Vossen et al., 2004) or by vaccination (Levin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a comparison with cited experimental studies.

claim: All close contacts with varicella patients were assumed to exert an equal 'average' boosting effect on the exposed individual.
source: A possible limitation of our study was that all close contacts with varicella patients were assumed to exert an equal 'average' boosting effect on the exposed individual.
evidence: This is a stated model assumption and limitation.

claim: The VZV reactivation probability was estimated to be 5% per week.
source: The VZV reactivation probability was estimated to be 5% per week.
evidence: This is a model-derived estimate.

claim: Observed data on VZV reactivation probability are rather sparse and highly divergent regarding study design, sampling site and results.
source: Observed data on VZV reactivation probability are rather sparse and highly divergent regarding study design, sampling site (saliva, blood, cerebrospinal fluid) and results (Schünemann et al., 1997; Mehta et al., 2003; Engelmann et al., 2008; Birlea et al., 2011; Nagel et al., 2011; van Velzen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature with citations.

claim: The observed weekly VZV reactivation probability varies between 0 and 71%.
source: The observed weekly VZV reactivation probability is a topic of discussion in the literature and varies between 0 and 71%.
evidence: This is a summary of literature findings.

claim: None of the best fitting parameter sets predicted a significant effect of VZV reactivation on VZV-CMI.
source: None of our best fitting parameter sets predicted a significant effect of VZV reactivation on VZV-CMI, implying that endogenous boosting most likely does not have an impact on the occurrence of HZ.
evidence: This is a model-derived finding.

claim: Endogenous boosting most likely does not have an impact on the occurrence of HZ.
source: None of our best fitting parameter sets predicted a significant effect of VZV reactivation on VZV-CMI, implying that endogenous boosting most likely does not have an impact on the occurrence of HZ.
evidence: This is an inference from the model results.

claim: The annual decline of VZV-CMI was predicted to be between 1 and 1.5%.
source: The annual decline of VZV-CMI was predicted to be between 1 and 1.5%.
evidence: This is a model-derived estimate.

claim: The predicted annual decline of VZV-CMI (1-1.5%) is lower than the 2.7–3.9% experimentally observed by Levin et al. for individuals older than 60 years.
source: This result is lower than the 2.7–3.9% experimentally observed by Levin et al. for individuals older than 60 years (Levin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a comparison with cited experimental data.

claim: The twofold difference in waning rate can be explained by the explicit disentanglement of waning and boosting.
source: The twofold difference in waning rate can be explained by the explicit disentanglement of waning and boosting (with younger age groups having—on average—higher probabilities of being boosted recently thereby actually increasing the observed waning rate).
evidence: This is an explanation for the difference between model and experimental results.

claim: The model predicts a net increase in HZ incidence during approximately 50 years following a 100% effective varicella vaccine given to all 1-year-old children.
source: Our predictions (averaged per parameter set) showed a net increase in HZ incidence during approximately 50 years (see Figure 4).
evidence: This is a model prediction shown in Figure 4.

claim: The delay in the HZ peak incidence is caused by cohorts born close to the time varicella vaccination was introduced experiencing less repeated boosting instances during their childhood than previously born cohorts.
source: This delay in the HZ peak incidence is caused by cohorts born close to the time varicella vaccination was introduced experiencing less repeated boosting instances during their childhood than previously born cohorts (a mechanism that is similar to the progressive immunity model proposed in the deterministic VZV model by Guzzetta et al. (2013)).
evidence: This is an explanation of the model mechanism with a citation to a similar model.

claim: Proper documentation of significant increases in HZ incidence might not be possible during the first 10 years, even if a 100% effective vaccine would be used.
source: However, our analysis shows that proper documentation of significant increases in HZ incidence might not be possible during the first 10 years, even if a 100% effective vaccine would be used.
evidence: This is an inference from the model results.

claim: During the first 10 years of the US program, both uptake and efficacy with the initial single dose vaccination programme were far below 100%.
source: For instance, during the first 10 years of the US program, both uptake and efficacy with the initial single dose vaccination programme were far below 100%.
evidence: This is a statement about the US vaccination program.

claim: The VZV IBM predicts that 31–40 year olds contribute the most to the peak in HZ incidence following varicella vaccination.
source: However, in contrast to earlier model estimates our VZV IBM predicts that 31–40 year olds contribute the most to the peak in HZ incidence following varicella vaccination.
evidence: This is a model prediction that contrasts with earlier models.

claim: Some observational studies found no effect of varicella vaccination on HZ incidence for those aged 60 years and older.
source: Some observational studies found no effect of varicella vaccination on HZ incidence for those aged 60 years and older (Hales et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a cited observational study.

claim: Younger adults have been shown to be less likely to develop post-herpetic neuralgia.
source: Importantly, younger adults have been shown to be less likely to develop post-herpetic neuralgia (Opstelten et al., 2002; Drolet et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Cost-effectiveness analyses using the VZV IBM would be more in favor of universal childhood varicella vaccination compared to deterministic models.
source: Thus although our aggregated predictions regarding the increase in HZ incidence following varicella vaccination may appear similar to those published using deterministic models, cost-effectiveness analyses using our VZV IBM would be more in favor of universal childhood varicella vaccination.
evidence: This is an inference about cost-effectiveness based on the model predictions.

claim: A major benefit of the modeling approach is the possibility to verify best–fit parameter values via experimental studies.
source: A major benefit of our modeling approach is the possibility to verify our best–fit parameter values via experimental studies, or vice versa, to adapt parameter values when empiricism delivers new insights.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the modeling approach.

claim: The dynamics of the synthetic population are based on Belgian population and mortality data normalized to a fixed total population of 998,400 individuals.
source: The dynamics of the synthetic population of the individual-based model are based on Belgian population and mortality data normalized to a fixed total population of 998,400 individuals (Eurostat, 2012).
evidence: This is a description of the model's demographic structure with a citation.

claim: The chosen population size is the result of a trade-off between ensuring sufficient heterogeneity and a manageable computational burden.
source: The chosen population size is the result of a trade-off between ensuring sufficient heterogeneity and a manageable computational burden.
evidence: This is an explanation of a modeling decision.

claim: Natural deaths are selected based on the age-dependent mortality rate.
source: Natural deaths are selected based on the age-dependent mortality rate.
evidence: This is a description of the model's demographic dynamics.

claim: Per time step, the number of newborns equals the number of deaths to obtain a constant population size.
source: Per time step, the number of newborns equals the number of deaths to obtain a constant population size.
evidence: This is a description of the model's demographic dynamics.

claim: The model runs in time steps of 1 week.
source: The model runs in time steps of 1 week and people with week-age 53 move to the next age class.
evidence: This is a description of the model's temporal resolution.

claim: At the start of the simulation, 30 individuals between ages 1 and 3 are randomly infected with CP.
source: At the start of the simulation, 30 individuals between ages 1 and 3 are randomly infected with CP.
evidence: This is a description of the model's initial conditions.

claim: The relative HZ infectiousness is empirically estimated to be 0.17.
source: with w(i,n) the weekly effective contact probability for an individual from group i with a random individual from group n, m the relative HZ infectiousness (empirically estimated to be 0.17 [cf. paragraph 'Modeling VZV endogenous reactivation'])
evidence: This is a model parameter based on empirical estimation.

claim: The VZV infection probability is based on empirical social contact data.
source: The VZV infection probability, w(i, n), is based on empirical social contact data as described elsewhere (Ogunjimi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a description of the model's contact structure with a citation.

claim: Individuals infected for the first time with VZV are infectious for 1 week after an incubation period of 2 weeks.
source: Individuals infected for the first time with VZV are infectious for 1 week after an incubation period of 2 weeks.
evidence: This is a model parameter based on known disease characteristics.

claim: CP recovered individuals receive a normalized CMI value of 1 ± a randomly distributed factor (normal distribution with variance 0.1).
source: Next, they are CP recovered and receive a normalized CMI value of 1 ± a randomly distributed factor (normal distribution with variance 0.1 as suggested by Terada et al. (1994)).
evidence: This is a model parameter with a citation.

claim: Once in the CP recovered state, VZV-CMI starts waning at a weekly rate via multiplication with (1—waning-rate).
source: Once arrived in the CP recovered state, VZV-CMI starts waning at a weekly rate via the multiplication with (1—waning-rate).
evidence: This is a description of the model's waning mechanism.

claim: The waning-rate is informed by the annual decline of 2.7–3.9% per age-year as noted by baseline VZV-CMI values by Levin et al.
source: The waning-rate (see Table 2) is informed by the annual decline of 2.7–3.9% per age-year as noted by baseline VZV-CMI values by Levin et al. (2008).
evidence: This is a model parameter informed by cited data.

claim: In the first 6 weeks after exogenous boosting, VZV-CMI is assumed to increase linearly up to 'Peak fold increase' times the pre-boosting value.
source: In the first 6 weeks after exogenous boosting, VZV-CMI is assumed to increase linearly up to 'Peak fold increase' times the pre-boosting value (Levin et al., 2008), but is limited to a maximum of 4 times the VZV-CMI value without re-exposure.
evidence: This is a model assumption with a citation.

claim: The effect of boosting is limited to a maximum of 4 times the VZV-CMI value without re-exposure.
source: In the first 6 weeks after exogenous boosting, VZV-CMI is assumed to increase linearly up to 'Peak fold increase' times the pre-boosting value (Levin et al., 2008), but is limited to a maximum of 4 times the VZV-CMI value without re-exposure.
evidence: This is a model constraint.

claim: Limiting the effect of boosting to a factor 4 is based on the finding that pediatricians, highly exposed to CP, have T-cell values that are on average 3–4 times higher than controls.
source: Limiting the effect of boosting to a factor 4 is based on the recent finding that pediatricians, highly exposed to CP, have T-cell values that are on average 3–4 times higher than controls, but not higher (Ogunjimi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a model constraint based on cited empirical data.

claim: The FoR defines the VZV-CMI needed to resist clinical reactivation.
source: The FoR defines the VZV-CMI needed to resist clinical reactivation and if VZV-CMI < FoR, reactivation will lead to HZ.
evidence: This is a description of a model concept.

claim: If VZV-CMI < FoR, reactivation will lead to HZ.
source: The FoR defines the VZV-CMI needed to resist clinical reactivation and if VZV-CMI < FoR, reactivation will lead to HZ.
evidence: This is a model rule.

claim: The FoR deviates per time step and individual by means of a gamma probability density function.
source: The FoR deviates per time step and individual by means of a gamma probability density function.
evidence: This is a description of the model's stochastic component.

claim: HZ individuals are assumed to be infectious for 1 week.

claim: HZ individuals receive a VZV-CMI reset to 1 ± random factor (normally distributed).
source: HZ individuals are assumed to be infectious for 1 week and receive a VZV-CMI reset to 1 ± random factor (normally distributed, cf. primary infection).

claim: The relative infectiousness of HZ patients was approximated by the relative infectiousness of breakthrough CP patients.
source: We chose to approximate the relative infectiousness of HZ patients by the relative infectiousness of breakthrough CP patients (Bernstein et al., 1993).

claim: The relative infectiousness of breakthrough CP patients has previously been estimated at 0.17.
source: This has previously been estimated at 0.17 (Brisson et al., 2002).

claim: Reinstallation of VZV-specific immunity after HZ is based on experimental data showing that a second case of HZ only occurs in about 5% of individuals.
source: Reinstallation of VZV-specific immunity after HZ is based on experimental data showing that a second case of HZ only occurs in about 5% of individuals (Yawn et al., 2011) and that VZV-CMI is higher in recovered HZ patients than in age-matched controls (Weinberg et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a model assumption based on cited experimental data.

claim: VZV-CMI is higher in recovered HZ patients than in age-matched controls.
source: Reinstallation of VZV-specific immunity after HZ is based on experimental data showing that a second case of HZ only occurs in about 5% of individuals (Yawn et al., 2011) and that VZV-CMI is higher in recovered HZ patients than in age-matched controls (Weinberg et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited experimental data.

claim: If VZV-CMI ≥ FoR, endogenous boosting occurs followed by an exponential decrease.
source: If VZV-CMI ≥ FoR, endogenous boosting occurs followed by an exponential decrease according to one of the scenarios described in the previous section.
evidence: This is a model rule.

claim: The peak following endogenous boosting is restricted to be at most equal to the peak following exogenous boosting.
source: The peak following endogenous boosting, however, is restricted to be at most equal to the peak following exogenous boosting.
evidence: This is a model constraint.

claim: An endogenous boosting sequence will always be overruled by a new successful exogenous re-exposure boosting episode.
source: In addition, we assume that an endogenous boosting sequence will always be overruled by a new successful exogenous re-exposure boosting episode.
evidence: This is a model assumption.

source: Simulations were performed using Matlab 2012b on the Flemish VSC supercomputer.

claim: Simulations ran for 320 years.
source: Simulations ran for 320 years and model output was obtained by averaging the age-specific results over the last 80 years.

claim: Model output was obtained by averaging the age-specific results over the last 80 years.
source: Simulations ran for 320 years and model output was obtained by averaging the age-specific results over the last 80 years.

source: The following 7 parameters were estimated by means of the fitting procedure: VZV-CMI waning rate, type of boosting scenario, duration of exogenous boosting, peak fold increase following exogenous boosting, VZV reactivation probability, FoR distribution and the peak fold increase following endogenous boosting.

source: We calculated per set the Binomial likelihood by fitting the HZ age-specific output data to Belgian HZ incidence data (Bilcke et al., 2012).
